subject: Agriculture
title: Biocontrol Gone Wrong
description: A fast breakdown of Biocontrol Gone Wrong for builders.

hook.text: Australia introduced cane toads in 1935 to eat beetles. The toads ignored the beetles and became the pest.

buildup.text: 102 cane toads were released in Queensland. Today, 200 million cover northern Australia, eating native wildlife.

discovery.text: Cane toads are poisonous to native predators, who die trying to eat them. Quolls and goannas are vanishing.

twist.text: This isn't unique. Mongoose introduced to Hawaii for rats now prey on endangered birds instead.

climax.text: Modern biocontrol uses host-specific agents tested for decades before release. The cane toad era taught harsh lessons.

punchline.text: Importing a predator without testing is releasing a problem to solve a problem.

quiz.question: Why did cane toad introduction in Australia fail as biocontrol?
options: Toads ignored the target beetles, became invasive, and poisoned native predators

details.summary: Biological control introductions have sometimes backfired catastrophically when the introduced predator attacked native species instead of or in addition to the target pest. This topic covers notorious failures like the cane toad in Australia and the mongoose in Hawaii.
details.whyItMatters: Failed biocontrol introductions have caused irreversible ecological damage and driven native species to extinction. These cautionary tales shaped modern biocontrol regulations that now require extensive safety testing before any release.
takeaways: Cane toads introduced to Australia in 1935 became an invasive pest themselves
The mongoose introduced to Hawaii decimated native bird populations instead of rats
Modern biocontrol requires years of host-specificity testing before release approval

faq.question: What went wrong with the cane toad introduction in Australia?
faq.answer: In 1935, Australia imported cane toads from Hawaii to control beetles in sugar cane fields. The toads couldn't reach the beetles on tall cane stalks and instead spread across the continent. They poison native predators that try to eat them and now number over 200 million.

faq.question: How has biocontrol regulation changed after these failures?
faq.answer: Modern biocontrol agents undergo years of quarantine testing to confirm they only attack the target pest. Host-range studies expose the agent to dozens of non-target species. International protocols require environmental impact assessments, and releases must be approved by government agencies.
